newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Battered dollar rallies, Euro shares wallow.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Battered dollar rallies, Euro shares wallow.

text.p: The dollar rallied in European trade on Thursday afternoon after tumbling by more than two yen overnight, while Europe's key bourses remained down after Wall Street opened weaker.
The U.S. currency fell to around 115.60 yen in Asia, its lowest level against the yen since December, and slipped further in European trade touching a low of around 114.70 yen before rallying.
Top-level Japanese officials jumped in to try and stem the dollar's freefall, saying the Group of Seven agreement reached in April had filtered through to the markets "sufficiently".
Such comments -- made by Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka and Eisuke Sakakibara, head of the finance ministry's international finance bureau -- had an effect, pulling the dollar off its lows.
But then comments by a leading Japanese politician sparked fresh speculation about higher Japanese interest rates.
The dollar's fall against they yen also dragged it dollar down against the mark, and although the market soon recovered from the initial shock, traders said the U.S. currency looked far from healthy.
"When dollar/yen fell on the interest rate remarks it triggered long-term stops all over the place, in dollar/mark as well," said one trader at a U.S. bank here.

Koichi Kato, secretary-general of Japan's ruling Liberal Democratic Party, was quoted by Jiji news agency as saying Japan may face pressure to change its current low interest rates as it progresses with financial market deregulation.
Kato's remark drove dollar down to 114.70 yen, its lowest since December 26, though it had rallied to around 116.20 by 1415 gmt.
Dollar/mark softened in tandem during the morning but then rallied and climbed a touch above Wednesday's close of 1.6965.
Analysts said that judging from dollar/yen's slight rebound, the market realised it had overreacted to Kato's comment.

"There is a view in the market that we're going to get a rate hike in Japan, although I think that's premature," said Nigel Richardson, international economist at Yamaichi International here. "So the market is very sensitive to that kind of comment right now, as it's not absolutely convinced it (a rate hike) is going to happen," Richardson said.
However, the dollar's rebound was small compared to its overnight plunge and the market was still nervous.

The market was also digesting the latest U.S. data which showed that consumer prices there advanced modestly in April, offering more proof that inflation remained largely in check. The U.S. Labour Department said the Consumer Price Index rose 0.1 percent last month, matching the 0.1 percent rise in March.

Behind the dollar's tumble overnight was speculation the U.S. would support a stronger yen, fuelled by talk a newsletter from a Washington-based consulting firm stated Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin was calling for a dollar/yen rate of 115. Subscribers to the newsletter denied receiving such a report.

Elsewhere, Europe's leading share markets remained in the red after Wall Street opened weaker. Earlier, investors were disappointed that Wall Street only ended 12 points higher on Wednesday much higher.
In London, the FTSE 100 slid on profit-taking at the start and was down 23.5 points, or 0.5 percent, at 4,666.2 at 1415 GMT. The market, Europe's biggest, has stormed higher in recent days.

"The overall tone of the (U.S.) numbers is disappointing. The rise in the core rate has shifted the pendulum in favour of the Fed tightening. But it's still a close call," said Nick Stamenkovic, economist with DKB International.
Shares in France and Germany also remained in the minus column in the wake of Wall Street's opening weakness.
In Paris the blue-chip CAC-40 index was down 7.99 points at 2,766.64, while in Frankfurt the DAX index was down 11.58 points at 3,562.11.
Gold prices came under pressure in Europe on market fears that Germany may revalue its gold reserves.
Germany's Ministry of Finance said that Finance Minister Theo Waigel would discuss a proposal to revalue the country's 2,956 tonnes of gold reserves at a Bundesbank Council meeting.

Reports of the proposal appeared on Wednesday evening and knocked about $2.00 per ounce off the gold price in New York. On Thursday afternoon gold was fixed at $346.40 per ounce, compared with $348.65 in late trade in London in Wednesday

Revaluing Germany's gold reserves closer to the market price than their 144-mark ($85.05) an ounce book value, would allow the government to release billions of "hidden" reserves to offset deficits and possibly avoid raising taxes.
STOCK PRICES AT 1415 GMT
London's FTSE 100 was down 20.7 points at 4,666.2.
The Paris CAC-40 index was down 6.52 points at 2,768.11.
Frankfurt's DAX index was down 11.58 points at 3,562.85.
CURRENCIES AT 1415 GMT
The dollar stood at 1.6992 marks in late trade compared with 1.6977 on Wednesday and 116.20 yen versus 118.83.
PRECIOUS METALS
Gold fixed at $346.40 after closing at $348.65 an ounce in London on Wednesday.
